user: Are wind tunnels useful in the design of airplanes?
assistant: Yes, wind tunnels are indeed very useful in the design of airplanes. The Altitude Wind Tunnel (AWT), the nation’s first wind tunnel capable of studying full-scale engines under realistic flight conditions, played a significant role in the development of early U.S. jet engines. The AWT’s post-war testing and improvement of axial-flow turbojet engines was the facility’s most enduring contribution to the aerospace field. Aircraft noise is a barrier to emerging aviation markets. A free-jet wind tunnel, plays a key role in evaluating jet noise reduction concepts. They provide a controlled environment where engineers can test various aspects of aircraft design. The 9-by 15-Foot Low-Speed Wind Tunnel, for example, is used for testing the takeoff, approach, and landing of aircraft in a continuous subsonic environment.
user: Does NASA use wind tunnels?
assistant: Yes, NASA extensively uses wind tunnels in its research and development. The AWT’s post-war testing and improvement of axial-flow turbojet engines was the facility’s most enduring contribution to the aerospace field. The facility first supported Project Mercury, then for a variety of tests of the Centaur upper stage rocket. Also, the 8-by-6 Foot Supersonic Wind Tunnel operates either in an aerodynamic closed-loop cycle, testing aerodynamic performance models, or in a open-loop cycle, testing full-scale models and components. The 9-by 15-Foot Low-Speed Wind Tunnel is the most utilized low-speed propulsion acoustic facility in the world, and it is the only national facility that can simulate takeoff, approach, and landing in a continuous subsonic environment. The Hypersonic Tunnel Facility (HTF) at NASA’s Neil A. Armstrong Test Facility is a hypersonic (Mach 5, 6, and 7) blowdown, nonvitiated freejet facility that tests large-scale hypersonic air-breathing propulsion systems. Additionally, the Icing Research Tunnel supports the development of tools and methods for simulating the growth of ice on aircraft surfaces as well as the development and certification of ice protection systems.
user: What else does NASA do?
assistant: Missions - NASA explores the unknown in air and space, innovates for the benefit of humanity, and inspires the world through discovery. NASA engages in a wide range of activities beyond the use of wind tunnels. Here are a few examples:

It is the only national facility that can simulate takeoff, approach, and landing in a continuous subsonic environment.  3. NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland provides ground test facilities to industry, government, and academia.  4. These are just a few examples of the diverse activities that NASA is involved in.
user: Is the Hubble Space Telescope still working?
assistant: Yes, the Hubble Space Telescope is still operational. It has observed some fascinating cosmic wonder every day of the year with a lens that provides astronomers with a powerful tool to extend our view into previously unseen regions of the universe. The Hubble Space Telescope has been operating for over three decades and continues to make ground-breaking discoveries that shape our fundamental understanding of the universe. Hubble is a project of international cooperation between NASA and ESA (European Space Agency). Designed and built in the 1970’s and 1980’s, Hubble has far surpassed its 15-year life expectancy and produced science never thought possible at the time of its launch.   Hubble continues to uncover the mysteries of the universe. Hubble has not only furthered our knowledge of the known universe, it's shocked the astronomical world with never-before-seen phenomena. 
user: How is the Hubble Telescoop going to be replaced.
assistant: NASA and its partners are launching the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) as a successor to the Hubble Space Telescope. Webb is the premier observatory of the next decade, serving thousands of astronomers worldwide. The JWST is designed to build upon the scientific achievements of the Hubble. Webb launched on Dec. 25th 2021. It does not orbit around the Earth like the Hubble Space Telescope, it orbits the Sun 1.5 million kilometers (1 million miles) away from the Earth. The James Webb Space Telescope will help to study the atmospheres of exoplanets.

And who was Hubble?
[The End of Current Turn Question]

[The Start of Reference Answer]
The Hubble Space Telescope is named after Edwin Powell Hubble, (1889 - 1953) American astronomer whose observations proved that galaxies are "island universes", not nebulae inside our own galaxy. His greatest discovery, called "Hubble's Law", was the linear relationship between a galaxy's distance and the speed with which it is moving. He is best known for demonstrating that there are many galaxies beyond the Milky Way and for discovering that the universe is expanding.
[The End of Reference Answer]
